entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Drest VII, a pivotal figure in the tumultuous Pictish succession struggles of the early 8th century, briefly held the kingship of the Picts from 724 to 726 CE. His ascent followed the unprecedented abdication of the powerful Nechtan mac Der-Ilei, marking a period of intense instability and dynastic conflict within Fortriu, the dominant Pictish kingdom. Drest's short reign is significant less for his direct achievements and more as a catalyst and casualty in the power vacuum that ultimately paved the way for the rise of Óengus I mac Fergusa, one of the most formidable Pictish monarchs. His brief tenure highlights the fragile nature of royal authority and the fierce competition among rival claimants to the Pictish throne during a critical transition period in early medieval Scotland.

Drest assumed the throne in 724 CE after King Nechtan mac Der-Ilei, who had ruled for approximately two decades, unexpectedly abdicated and retired to a monastery. This abdication immediately triggered a fierce power struggle among several claimants, including Nechtan's own kinsmen and others like Alpín mac Echdach. Drest's grip on power was tenuous, and he faced immediate challenges. In 726, he was overthrown and imprisoned by Alpín, who then claimed the kingship. This coup was short-lived, as Nechtan mac Der-Ilei briefly returned from monastic life in 728 to reclaim his throne, further destabilizing the realm and leading to the Battle of Monithcrup where Drest and Alpín were among the defeated.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Drest VII's short, turbulent reign and his subsequent elimination were crucial in the violent Pictish succession crisis of the 720s, directly contributing to the rise of Óengus I mac Fergusa, who established a more powerful and stable Pictish kingdom for decades.
